title: Variables and Constants
theory: In Swift, safety and clarity are priorities. We use 'let' to define constants (values that never change after the first assignment) and 'var' for variables (values that can be changed). Apple's official recommendation is: use 'let' by default whenever possible. Switch to 'var' only if the compiler requires it or if you are sure the value will need to change.
corporateCase: In a banking app, the 'Transaction ID' or the 'User's CPF' are declared with 'let', since they should never change. The 'Current Balance', on the other hand, is declared with 'var', since it changes with every transaction.
gameCase: In a platformer game, gravity ('let gravity = 9.8') and the maximum health limit ('let maxHealth = 100') are constants. The character's current position ('var positionY') and current health ('var currentHealth') are variables.

quiz.question: What is Apple's official recommendation about using let and var?
options: Use var for everything to avoid compile errors
Use let by default and switch to var only when necessary
Use let only for numbers and var for text
quiz.explanation: Apple recommends 'let' by default to ensure immutability, which makes code safer, more predictable and optimized by the compiler.

quiz.question: What happens if you try to change the value of a constant (let)?
options: The compiler raises an error saying that 'let' cannot be reassigned
The old value is erased from memory
quiz.explanation: The Swift compiler prevents reassignment of constants, ensuring safety at compile time.

quiz.question: Why does the Swift compiler prefer constants (let)?
options: Because they take up fewer lines of code
Because they enable memory and performance optimizations
Because they are easier to read
Because Swift does not support global variables
quiz.explanation: Knowing that a value will not change allows the compiler to optimize memory usage and execution speed.

quiz.question: Which of the options below MUST be a variable (var)?
options: The base URL of an API
The maximum number of login attempts allowed
The text currently typed into a search field
quiz.explanation: The search text changes with every key the user presses, so it must be mutable.

quiz.question: How does Swift handle typing when using let or var without explicitly declaring the type?
options: It raises an error requiring the type
It infers the type based on the assigned value
It assumes it is a String
quiz.explanation: Swift has Type Inference, automatically deducing the type from the initial value.

extraQuiz.question: What is the main advantage of using 'let' in multithreaded environments?
options: None, 'let' does not work in multithreaded code
It ensures the value will not be changed simultaneously by different threads (Thread Safety)
It lets several threads change the value faster
extraQuiz.explanation: Constants are immutable, so they are safe to be read by multiple threads simultaneously with no risk of race conditions.

extraQuiz.question: How do you declare multiple constants on the same line?
extraQuiz.explanation: You can declare multiple constants or variables on the same line by separating them with commas.

extraQuiz.question: Can you declare a constant without an initial value and assign it later?
options: No, constants must be initialized at declaration
Yes, as long as the type is explicitly declared and the value is assigned exactly once before use
Yes, and it can be reassigned later
extraQuiz.explanation: Swift allows late initialization of constants, as long as the compiler can prove it will receive a value before first use and will never be changed afterward.

extraQuiz.question: What does the word 'var' mean in Swift?
extraQuiz.explanation: 'var' is short for Variable, indicating a value that can vary/change.

extraQuiz.question: What is the recommended naming convention for variables and constants in Swift?
extraQuiz.explanation: Apple recommends camelCase (e.g., myVariable) for properties, variables and constants.

title: Optionals
theory: Optionals are one of Swift's most powerful features. They represent two possibilities: either a value exists (Some) or there is no value at all (nil). They are declared by adding a '?' after the type. Swift's golden rule is: avoid using 'force unwrap' (!) unless you are 100% sure the value is not nil, since this will crash the app.
corporateCase: In an e-commerce sign-up form, the address 'Complement' field is optional. In code, it is represented as 'var complemento: String?'. If the user does not fill it in, the value will be 'nil'.
gameCase: In an RPG, the player may or may not have a weapon equipped. This is modeled as 'var armaEquipada: Arma?'. If it is 'nil', the player attacks bare-handed.

exercises.hint: Use the symbol that means 'may or may not have a value'.

exercises.hint: In Swift, the absence of a value is represented by a 3-letter word.

quiz.question: What is an Optional in Swift?
options: A kind of variable that can change type
A container that can hold a value or be nil
A function that can be ignored
quiz.explanation: An Optional is essentially an Enum with two cases: .some(Wrapped) and .none (nil).

quiz.question: What happens if you use force unwrap (!) on an Optional that contains 'nil'?
options: The value becomes 0 or an empty string
The compiler warns, but it runs
Swift ignores the line of code
quiz.explanation: Force unwrap tries to extract the value by force. If there is no value (nil), the program breaks immediately.

quiz.question: Why does Swift use Optionals instead of allowing any variable to be null (as in Objective-C or Java)?
options: To make the code more complex
To force the developer to explicitly deal with the absence of a value, increasing safety
quiz.explanation: By making nullability explicit in the type system, Swift forces the programmer to handle the 'nil' case, eliminating most NullPointerExceptions.

quiz.question: What is the default value of an Optional variable declared as 'var nome: String?' if no value is assigned?
quiz.explanation: Optional variables (var) are automatically initialized with 'nil' if no value is provided.

quiz.question: How does Swift represent an Optional internally?
options: As a generic Enum with .some and .none cases
quiz.explanation: Optional is an enum in the Swift standard library: enum Optional<Wrapped> { case none, case some(Wrapped) }.

title: Unwrapping
theory: To safely use the value inside an Optional, we need to 'unwrap' it. 'if let' creates a new temporary constant available only inside the if block. 'guard let' does the opposite: it checks whether there is a value, and if there is not, it forces an exit from the function (early exit with return). The big advantage of 'guard let' is that the unwrapped variable stays available in the rest of the function's scope, avoiding excessive nesting (pyramid of doom).
corporateCase: When processing login, we use 'guard let token = response.token else { showError(); return }'. If the token exists, we continue the normal login flow without nesting the code.
gameCase: Before applying damage, we check: 'guard let alvo = inimigoAtual else { return }'. If no enemy is selected, the attack function is interrupted immediately.

exercises.question: Use the control structure to safely unwrap within a closed scope
exercises.hint: Used to run a block of code only if the value exists.

exercises.question: Use the structure for early exit
exercises.hint: Protects the function, requiring the condition to be true in order to continue.

exercises.question: Complete the guard let with the keyword needed to exit the function
exercises.hint: You must exit the current scope if the guard fails.

exercises.question: Unwrap multiple variables in the same if let (separator)
exercises.codeSnippet: if let x = opX ___ let y = opY { }
exercises.hint: Use a comma to separate multiple unwrapping conditions.

exercises.question: Which word goes with guard let to define the failure block?

quiz.question: What is the main scope difference between 'if let' and 'guard let'?
options: The 'if let' variable is available outside the block, the 'guard let' one is not
The 'guard let' variable is available in the outer scope after the declaration, the 'if let' one is restricted to the block
Both are restricted to their blocks
quiz.explanation: 'guard let' is designed for the 'happy path', making the unwrapped variable available for the rest of the function.

quiz.question: What is required inside the 'else' block of a 'guard let'?
options: A control transfer that exits the current scope (return, break, continue, throw)
quiz.explanation: The compiler requires the guard's else block to stop the current flow, ensuring the code below does not run with invalid data.

quiz.question: What is the problem known as the 'Pyramid of Doom'?
options: Multiple nested 'if let' statements that push the code far to the right, making it hard to read
quiz.explanation: Excessive nesting of 'if let' creates a pyramid-shaped structure. 'guard let' solves this by keeping the code left-aligned.

quiz.question: Is it possible to use 'guard let' outside of a function or loop?
options: No, it requires a context it can 'exit' from (such as a function, loop or closure)
quiz.explanation: Since guard requires a 'return', 'break', etc., it must be inside a scope that supports those exit statements.

quiz.question: How do you unwrap an Optional and check a boolean condition at the same time?
quiz.explanation: In Swift, you can combine Optional Binding (if let) with boolean conditions by separating them with commas.

title: Type Inference
theory: Swift is smart enough to deduce (infer) the type of a variable or constant based on the initial value you assign to it. This means you do not need to write the type explicitly most of the time. For example, 'let numero = 42' is automatically inferred as 'Int'. An explicit type annotation (e.g., 'let numero: Double = 42') is only needed when you do not provide an initial value, when the inferred type is not what you want, or to speed up compilation in very complex expressions.
corporateCase: When decoding JSON from a financial API, we use type inference to keep the code clean: 'let taxaJuros = 12.5' (inferred as Double).
gameCase: When initializing the game state: 'let isGameOver = false' (inferred as Bool), 'let playerName = "Hero"' (inferred as String).

exercises.question: What is the inferred type for: let vidas = 3
What is the inferred type for: let preco = 19.99
exercises.hint: Floating-point numbers are inferred as Double by default in Swift.

exercises.question: Provide the explicit type annotation to force a Float
What is the inferred type for: let mensagem = "Olá"
What is the inferred type for: let ativo = true

quiz.question: What is Type Inference in Swift?
options: The automatic conversion from String to Int
The compiler's ability to deduce a variable's type from its initial value
quiz.explanation: The compiler analyzes the value provided at initialization and sets the variable's type automatically.

quiz.question: If you declare 'let valor = 42.0', what type will Swift infer?
quiz.explanation: In Swift, any numeric literal with a decimal point is inferred as Double by default, since it offers greater precision.

quiz.question: When is an explicit type annotation (e.g., var nome: String) REQUIRED?
options: When the variable is declared without an initial value
quiz.explanation: If there is no initial value, the compiler has no way to guess the type, so you must specify it.

quiz.question: Does Swift allow changing a variable's type after it has been inferred? (e.g., var x = 10; x = "Olá")
options: Only if you use the word 'mutating'
Yes, but it raises a warning
quiz.explanation: Swift is Type-Safe. Once the type is set (inferred or explicit), it cannot be changed.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of Type Inference?
options: It makes the code cleaner and less verbose without losing the safety of strong typing
It makes the app run faster
It lets you mix types freely
It avoids the use of Optionals
quiz.explanation: You write less code (without cluttering it with obvious types), but the compiler still ensures that all type rules are followed.

title: Value vs Reference Types
theory: In Swift, types are divided into two categories. Value Types, such as Structs, Enums, Int, String and Array, are copied when assigned to a new variable or passed to a function. Each copy is independent. Reference Types, such as Classes, share the same instance in memory. If you change the copy, the original changes too. Apple strongly recommends using Structs (Value Types) to model data, since they avoid shared-state bugs.
corporateCase: The user profile (UserProfile) is a Struct. If you pass the profile to the edit screen, a copy is made. If the user cancels the edit, the original profile in the local database remains intact.
gameCase: An enemy's coordinates (Position) are a Struct. The game's level manager (LevelManager), which controls global state and needs to be accessed by several systems, is a Class.

exercises.question: Which keyword creates a Value Type to model complex data?
Which keyword creates a Reference Type?
exercises.hint: Used when you need shared identity.

exercises.question: In Swift, are Arrays and Dictionaries Value Types or Reference Types?
exercises.hint: They are implemented as Structs in the standard library.

exercises.question: To modify a property inside a method of a Struct, which keyword is needed before 'func'?
exercises.hint: Structs are immutable by default in their methods.

exercises.question: If 'A' is a class, and we do 'let B = A', is B a copy or a ___?
exercises.hint: It points to the same location in memory.

quiz.question: What happens when you assign an instance of a Struct to a new variable?
options: Both variables point to the same memory space
An independent, complete copy of the instance is created
quiz.explanation: Structs are Value Types. Assignment creates an exact copy, and changes to the copy do not affect the original.

quiz.question: What is Apple's main recommendation about using Structs and Classes?
options: Use Structs by default and Classes only when you need inheritance or shared identity
Use Structs only for math and Classes for UI
Do not use Structs in Swift
quiz.explanation: Structs are safer (no accidental shared state) and more performant (allocated on the Stack).

quiz.question: If you have a 'let' that stores a Class, can you change that class's internal properties (var)?
options: No, because the instance was declared with let
Yes, because 'let' on reference types protects only the memory reference, not the object's contents
Only if you use the word mutating
quiz.explanation: With Reference Types, 'let' means you cannot point to ANOTHER instance, but you can modify the internal properties of the current instance.

quiz.question: If you have a 'let' that stores a Struct, can you change that Struct's internal properties (var)?
options: No, because the entire Struct becomes immutable
Only if the Struct inherits from NSObject
quiz.explanation: With Value Types, if the instance is 'let', all of its properties also become immutable, even if they were declared as 'var' in the Struct's definition.

quiz.question: How does Swift optimize copying large Value Types, such as Arrays with thousands of items?
options: It does not optimize, copying is always slow
It converts to a Class automatically
It uses the Copy-on-Write (CoW) technique, copying the memory only if the array is modified
It limits the size of the Array
quiz.explanation: Copy-on-Write ensures that copying collections is extremely fast, since actual duplication in memory only happens at the moment one of the copies is changed.

title: Nil Coalescing and Optional Chaining
theory: The Nil Coalescing operator (??) lets you provide a default value in case an Optional is nil, safely unwrapping it in a single line. Optional Chaining (?.) lets you safely access properties, methods or subscripts of an Optional. If the Optional is nil, the call fails silently and returns nil, instead of causing a crash. Together, they make Swift code extremely concise and safe.
corporateCase: When loading the profile picture: 'let urlImagem = usuario.fotoPerfil?.url ?? urlPadrao'. If the user has no photo, we use the system's default image.
gameCase: When trying to play the equipped weapon's sound: 'player.armaEquipada?.tocarSomDeTiro()'. If the player is unarmed (armaEquipada is nil), nothing happens and the game does not break.

exercises.question: Provide the default value "Anonymous" in case the name is nil
Safely access the 'rua' property of the optional address
Call the 'atacar()' method only if the enemy exists
Set the balance to 0.0 if it is nil
Chain the access: empresa -> ceo -> nome

quiz.question: What does the Nil Coalescing operator (??) do?
options: Forces the unwrapping of an Optional
Checks whether two Optionals are equal
Unwraps an Optional if it has a value, or returns a default value if it is nil
quiz.explanation: It is an elegant way of saying 'use this value, but if it is nil, use this other default value'.

quiz.question: What is the return type of an expression that uses Optional Chaining (?.)?
options: Always an Optional, even if the accessed property is not optional
quiz.explanation: Since the chain can fail at any point and return nil, the final result of an Optional Chaining is always wrapped in an Optional.

quiz.question: What happens on the line 'let x = obj?.metodoQueRetornaInt() ?? 0' if 'obj' is nil?
options: The method is called and returns 0
The method call is ignored and 'x' receives 0
quiz.explanation: Optional Chaining fails silently, returning nil. Nil Coalescing catches that nil and supplies the default value 0.

quiz.question: Is it possible to chain multiple Optional Chainings? (e.g., a?.b?.c?.d)
options: No, the limit is one per line
Yes, and if any one of them is nil, the entire expression immediately returns nil
Yes, but it causes a memory leak
Only in Classes, not in Structs
quiz.explanation: Multiple chaining is one of Swift's biggest advantages, allowing you to safely navigate complex data hierarchies.

quiz.question: What is the difference between '??' and '!'?
options: None, they do the same thing
'??' provides a safe fallback, '!' forces extraction and crashes if nil
quiz.explanation: '??' is the safe, recommended alternative for dealing with missing values when you have an acceptable default value.

title: Enums (Associated Values)
theory: Enums (Enumerations) in Swift are first-class types. Unlike other languages where enums are just integers in disguise, in Swift they can have methods, computed properties and, most importantly, Associated Values. This allows each enum case to carry additional data of different types, making them perfect for modeling complex states.
corporateCase: Modeling network results: 'enum Result { case success(Data), case failure(Error) }'. The success case carries the actual data, the failure case carries the error.
gameCase: States of an NPC: 'enum NPCState { case idle, case walking(destination: Point), case attacking(target: Player, damage: Int) }'. The attacking state carries who the target is and how much damage it does.

exercises.question: Declare the keyword to create an enumeration
exercises.codeSnippet: ___ Direcao { case norte, sul, leste, oeste }

exercises.question: Add an associated value of type String to the 'erro' case
Which control structure is most used to evaluate Enums in Swift?
exercises.hint: Swift requires this structure to be exhaustive.

exercises.question: Extract the associated value in a switch case using let
exercises.hint: You 'bind' the associated value to a constant.

exercises.question: How do you access an Enum case when the type is already inferred?

quiz.question: What makes Enums in Swift more powerful than in languages like C?
options: They can have Associated Values, methods and computed properties
quiz.explanation: Enums in Swift are complex types that can encapsulate logic and data specific to each case.

quiz.question: What is an 'Associated Value' in an Enum?
options: An integer that represents the case
Extra information of any type that is attached to a specific enum case at creation time
quiz.explanation: Associated values let the enum carry the 'context' of the current state, such as the error code in a failure case.

quiz.question: What does the Swift compiler require when using a 'switch' with an Enum?
options: The switch must have at most 3 cases
The switch must be exhaustive, that is, cover all possible cases of the Enum
The switch must return a value
The switch cannot use the word 'default'
quiz.explanation: Exhaustiveness ensures you never forget to handle a new case added to the Enum in the future, preventing bugs.

quiz.question: Are Enums in Swift Value Types or Reference Types?
options: It depends on whether they have methods
quiz.explanation: Just like Structs, Enums are Value Types and are copied by value.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Raw Values and Associated Values in Enums?
options: Raw Values are predefined and the same for all instances of that case; Associated Values are defined when the instance is created and can vary
Raw Values only accept Int, Associated Values only accept String
quiz.explanation: Raw Values (e.g., case norte = "N") are static constants. Associated Values (e.g., case erro(codigo: 404)) are dynamic.

title: Closures and Defer
theory: Closures are self-contained blocks of code that can be passed around and used in your code (similar to lambdas in other languages). They capture and store references to variables from the context where they were created. If a closure is called after the function that created it returns (as in asynchronous requests), it must be marked with '@escaping'. 'defer' is a statement that postpones the execution of a block of code until the exact moment before the current scope exits, making it ideal for resource cleanup.
corporateCase: In API calls: 'api.fetchData { result in ... }'. The closure handles the asynchronous response. We use 'defer { stopLoadingAnimation() }' at the start of the function to make sure the spinner stops spinning, no matter whether the function ends in success or error.
gameCase: When starting an attack animation: 'animator.play(anim) { onAttackComplete() }'. The closure is the callback. We use 'defer { isAttacking = false }' to make sure the player's state is reset even if the function is interrupted early.

exercises.question: Which keyword postpones the execution of a block until the end of the scope?
How do you mark a closure that outlives the end of the function (e.g., asynchronous)?
What is the syntax for separating the parameters from the closure body?
exercises.hint: Keyword that marks the start of the closure body.

exercises.question: How do you refer to the first implicit parameter of a short closure?
To avoid Retain Cycles (memory leaks) when capturing 'self' in closures, we use [___ self]

quiz.question: What is a Closure in Swift?
options: A block of code that can be passed around like a variable and captures values from its context
quiz.explanation: Closures are functional blocks that capture the surrounding environment, enabling callbacks and asynchronous programming.

quiz.question: When is the block of code inside a 'defer' executed?
options: At the exact moment before execution leaves the current scope (function, loop, if)
quiz.explanation: defer guarantees that cleanup code (closing files, resetting states) runs regardless of how the function ends (return, throw, or natural end).

quiz.question: Why do we need to use '@escaping' on some closures passed as parameters?
options: To make the closure run faster
To tell the compiler that the closure will be stored and executed AFTER the function returns, requiring care with memory (self)
To allow the closure to modify variables
quiz.explanation: Non-escaping closures (the default) are destroyed when the function ends. Escaping closures outlive the function, which can cause memory leaks if they capture 'self' strongly.

quiz.question: What does the '$0' syntax mean in a closure?
options: The first parameter passed to the closure (Shorthand Argument Name)
quiz.explanation: Swift provides shorthand argument names ($0, $1, $2...) for inline closures, allowing you to omit the explicit declaration of the parameters.

quiz.question: If you have multiple 'defer' blocks in the same function, in what order are they executed?
options: In the order they were written (Top-to-Bottom)
In the reverse order they were written (Bottom-to-Top / LIFO)
Only the last one is executed
quiz.explanation: defer blocks work like a stack (Stack). The last defer declared is the first to run when exiting the scope.

title: Architecture Patterns (MVVM)
theory: The MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel) pattern is widely adopted in the Apple ecosystem, especially with SwiftUI. It separates business logic and state (ViewModel) from the user interface (View) and the data (Model). This makes testing, maintenance and code reuse easier. The View only observes the ViewModel and reacts to state changes, while the ViewModel processes user intents and updates the Model.
corporateCase: In a banking app, the 'ExtratoView' only displays the list of transactions. The 'ExtratoViewModel' is responsible for fetching data from the API, formatting dates and monetary values, and exposing a ready-made list for the View to consume.
gameCase: In a card game, the 'CardView' shows the card. The 'GameViewModel' manages the game rules, whose turn it is, and updates the score. The View simply reflects the ViewModel's current state.

exercises.question: Which layer in MVVM is responsible for formatting data for display?
exercises.hint: It sits between the Model and the View.

exercises.question: In SwiftUI, which property wrapper is commonly used in the ViewModel to notify the View about changes?
Should the View contain complex business logic?
exercises.hint: The View should be as 'dumb' as possible.

exercises.question: Which protocol does the ViewModel usually adopt in SwiftUI to be observable?
Should the Model import the UIKit or SwiftUI framework?
exercises.hint: The Model should be independent of UI.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of the MVVM pattern?
options: It separates presentation logic from the interface, making testing and maintenance easier
It is the only pattern supported by Apple
quiz.explanation: Separation of concerns lets you test the ViewModel without having to instantiate the View.

quiz.question: In MVVM, who 'owns' the ViewModel?
quiz.explanation: The View owns and observes the ViewModel. The ViewModel does not know who the View is.

quiz.question: What does the ViewModel do when the Model's data changes?
options: It updates the View directly by calling the View's methods
It notifies observers (such as the View) that the state has changed
quiz.explanation: The ViewModel uses data binding (such as @Published in Combine/SwiftUI) to notify the View reactively.

quiz.question: Which Apple framework is often used together with MVVM for reactive data binding?
quiz.explanation: Combine provides a declarative API for processing values over time, perfect for connecting ViewModels and Views.

quiz.question: In an MVVM app, where would you make a network call (API)?
options: In the ViewModel (or in a Service called by the ViewModel)
quiz.explanation: The ViewModel orchestrates business logic, delegating network calls to services and updating its state with the result.

title: Concurrency (async/await)
theory: Structured concurrency in Swift (introduced in Swift 5.5) uses 'async' and 'await' to write asynchronous code that is as easy to read as synchronous code. This replaces nested callbacks and improves safety and performance. 'Task' is used to start an asynchronous context from synchronous code. 'Actors' protect mutable state against data races in concurrent environments.
corporateCase: When logging in, we use 'let user = await api.login(credenciais)'. The code pauses on that line without freezing the interface (main thread) until the response arrives.
gameCase: When loading the assets of a heavy level: 'await loadTextures()'. A loading screen is displayed while the main thread stays free to animate the loading.

exercises.question: Which keyword marks a function as asynchronous?
exercises.hint: It comes before the return type.

exercises.question: Which keyword is used to pause execution until an asynchronous function finishes?
How do you start an asynchronous block of code from a synchronous context (such as viewDidLoad)?
exercises.hint: It represents a unit of asynchronous work.

exercises.question: Which reference type protects its internal state against concurrent access (data races)?
exercises.hint: Similar to a class, but safe for concurrency.

exercises.question: If an asynchronous function can fail (throw errors), how do we call it?

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of async/await compared to completion closures?
options: It avoids the 'pyramid of doom' (nested callbacks) and makes the control flow more linear and readable
It does not need an internet connection
quiz.explanation: Asynchronous code looks synchronous, making it easier to use try/catch and traditional loops.

quiz.question: What happens to the current thread when the code reaches an 'await'?
options: The thread is blocked (frozen) until the operation finishes
The thread is suspended and freed to run other work while it waits for the result
quiz.explanation: This is called 'suspension'. The thread does not sit idle; it can be used by other system tasks.

quiz.question: What is an Actor in Swift?
options: A reference type that isolates its state, ensuring that only one task accesses its data at a time, preventing data races
quiz.explanation: Actors provide built-in synchronization, replacing the need for manual locks or GCD serial queues.

quiz.question: Where should the User Interface (UI) update code run?
quiz.explanation: All UI updates on Apple platforms must happen on the main thread. @MainActor ensures this in modern Swift.

quiz.question: How do you run multiple asynchronous tasks in parallel and wait for all of them to finish?
quiz.explanation: 'async let' lets you start several tasks concurrently and wait for their results together.

title: Memory Management (ARC)
theory: Swift uses Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) to manage the app's memory. ARC tracks how many strong references exist for each class instance. When the count reaches zero, the memory is freed. The biggest danger is 'Retain Cycles', where two objects hold strong references to each other, preventing the count from reaching zero and causing a memory leak. We use 'weak' or 'unowned' to break these cycles.
corporateCase: A 'ViewController' has a strong reference to a 'ViewModel'. If the ViewModel has a closure that captures the ViewController strongly, we have a Retain Cycle. We solve it by capturing '[weak self]' in the closure.
gameCase: A 'Player' has a strong reference to its 'Weapon'. The 'Weapon' needs to know who its owner is, but uses a 'weak var owner: Player?' reference so as not to create a cycle.

exercises.question: What is the mechanism Swift uses to manage memory?
Which keyword creates a weak reference that can become nil?
Which keyword creates a weak reference that is NOT an Optional (it is assumed it will never be nil during use)?
How do you capture 'self' weakly inside a closure?
exercises.hint: It avoids retain cycles in closures.

exercises.question: By default, are references in Swift strong or weak?

quiz.question: What is a Retain Cycle?
options: An infinite loop in the code
When two objects hold strong references to each other, preventing ARC from freeing them from memory
quiz.explanation: Since both have a retain count of at least 1, ARC never destroys them, causing a Memory Leak.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'weak' and 'unowned'?
options: 'weak' creates an Optional that becomes nil when the object is destroyed. 'unowned' is not an Optional and crashes if accessed after the object is destroyed
quiz.explanation: Use 'weak' when the referenced object may have a shorter lifetime. Use 'unowned' when you are sure the referenced object will always exist as long as the reference exists.

quiz.question: Does ARC apply to Structs and Enums?
options: No, ARC manages only instances of Classes (Reference Types)
quiz.explanation: Value Types (Structs, Enums) are allocated on the Stack or inline and do not need reference counting, since they are copied.

quiz.question: What happens if you access an 'unowned' reference after the object has been deallocated?
quiz.explanation: Similar to force unwrap (!), accessing an invalid unowned reference breaks the app.

quiz.question: What is the common delegation pattern (Delegate Pattern) with regard to memory?
options: The delegate is always a strong reference
The delegate must be a Struct
The 'delegate' property is usually declared as 'weak' to avoid retain cycles
quiz.explanation: Since object A (e.g., TableView) belongs to object B (e.g., ViewController), if A has a strong delegate to B, a cycle forms. That is why delegates are 'weak'.

title: Protocol-Oriented Programming (POP)
theory: Swift was designed as a protocol-oriented language. Instead of inheriting behaviors from a superclass (OOP), you adopt protocols. This solves multiple inheritance problems and tight coupling. Protocol Extensions let you provide default implementations, bringing superpowers to Structs and Enums.
corporateCase: We have a banking app with several 'Error' views. Instead of inheriting from a BaseErrorViewController, we create an 'ErrorPresentable' protocol with a default extension that shows the alert, applicable to any ViewController.
gameCase: Characters and Enemies can attack. Instead of a 'Combatant' class, we use 'Attackable' and 'Damageable' protocols. An explosive barrel can be 'Damageable' without being an enemy.

exercises.question: What lets you give a protocol a default behavior?
Can Structs inherit from classes?

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of Protocol-Oriented Programming over classic inheritance?
options: It allows inheritance from multiple sources via composition and works with Value Types
It is the only way to use SwiftUI
quiz.explanation: POP allows flexible composition and works perfectly with Structs, avoiding the problems of deep class inheritance.

title: Generics
theory: Generics let you write flexible, reusable code that works with any type, while keeping type safety (Type Safety). Instead of writing separate functions for Int, String and Float, you write one function with a placeholder '<T>'. Arrays and Optionals in Swift are built using Generics under the hood.
corporateCase: An API service 'NetworkManager' that fetches and decodes data. Instead of having 'fetchUser' and 'fetchTransaction', we use 'func fetch<T: Decodable>(type: T.Type) -> T'.
gameCase: An inventory system that needs to store weapons, potions or armor. We use a generic 'struct Inventory<Element>' to store and organize any type of game item.

exercises.question: How do we define a generic function in Swift?
exercises.codeSnippet: func swapTwoValues___(_ a: inout T, _ b: inout T)

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the 'T: Equatable' constraint in a Generic?
options: To say that T is a number
To ensure that elements of type T can be compared with '=='
To ensure that T is not nil
quiz.explanation: Constraints in generics ensure the type passed in meets certain requirements, such as protocol conformance (e.g., Equatable).

title: Lifecycle (UIKit vs SwiftUI)
theory: An app's lifecycle defines how it starts, goes to the background and comes back. In the past, the AppDelegate managed everything. Later, the SceneDelegate appeared for multiple windows (iPadOS). In SwiftUI, we use the 'App' struct and the @main wrapper. Understanding these states is essential for saving data, pausing audio and saving battery.
corporateCase: A finance app hides the balance and shows a bank logo (blur) as soon as the app enters 'background', to prevent the information from leaking in the iOS multitasking screen.
gameCase: A game automatically pauses and saves the player's progress when they receive a phone call, triggering the 'sceneWillResignActive' state.

exercises.question: In SwiftUI, which modifier detects changes in the app's state?
exercises.hint: When it goes to the background.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'willResignActive' and 'didEnterBackground'?
options: None, they are the same state
willResignActive is when the app is permanently closed
willResignActive happens when an interruption arises (e.g., a phone call), but the app is still on screen. didEnterBackground is when it disappears completely
didEnterBackground only exists on the Mac
quiz.explanation: willResignActive is a transitional (inactive) state, whereas didEnterBackground means the app is running in the background (invisible).

title: SwiftUI and UIKit Interoperability
theory: Although SwiftUI is the future, many apps have UIKit codebases. To use a SwiftUI View in UIKit, you use 'UIHostingController'. To use a UIKit view in SwiftUI, we create a struct that adopts 'UIViewRepresentable' or 'UIViewControllerRepresentable'.
corporateCase: A company has had a complex QR Code reader built in UIKit for 5 years. They build the new screen in SwiftUI, but use a UIViewControllerRepresentable to wrap the old reader and save months of refactoring.
gameCase: A main menu built entirely and quickly in SwiftUI, which, when 'Play' is tapped, presents the heavy engine running in a UIViewController based on Metal or SpriteKit.

exercises.question: Which protocol wraps a native UIView for SwiftUI?

quiz.question: What does the 'Coordinator' do in UIViewRepresentable?
options: Communicates UIKit delegates and events back to SwiftUI
quiz.explanation: The Coordinator acts as a bridge, adopting UIKit delegate protocols to update state in SwiftUI.

title: watchOS & HealthKit
theory: watchOS demands fast designs and short interactions (glances), and focuses on health. watchOS apps today are independent. HealthKit is the central framework that consolidates the user's health data (with strict permissions) and lets apps read/write workouts, heart rate, etc.
corporateCase: A telemedicine app reads the user's average heart rate via HealthKit on the Apple Watch and alerts the doctor if it detects severe anomalies during the week.
gameCase: An RPG-style game ('Zombies, Run!') uses pedometer data from HealthKit via Apple Watch to advance the narrative and flee from monsters in the virtual game.

exercises.question: What must the app request before reading HealthKit data?

quiz.question: What is the best UI practice on watchOS?
options: Long texts to read and small buttons
Direct information, high contrast, quick actions and complications on the watch face
Always require the iPhone to be connected
quiz.explanation: Interactions on the Watch should last seconds. The focus is on legibility and immediate access to the main action.

title: macOS (AppKit and SwiftUI)
theory: macOS has a different paradigm: multiple floating windows, a menu bar, trackpad vs mouse, deep keyboard shortcuts. AppKit was the historical standard, but SwiftUI now unifies development, allowing you to build the iOS app for Mac (via Mac Catalyst or a Native Destination).
corporateCase: A code editor on the Mac uses 'Menu Bar' commands for main actions and global shortcuts, offering a native macOS multi-tab preferences window.
gameCase: On macOS, a game converts touch controls (virtual joysticks) to keyboard (WASD) and mouse click, actively handling window resizing by the user.

exercises.question: Which traditional framework builds interfaces on the Mac?

quiz.question: In SwiftUI for macOS, how do you create a top command bar?
options: Using the .commands modifier and CommandMenu inside the App block
quiz.explanation: The @main declaration provides the 'WindowGroup' scene, to which you attach '.commands { CommandMenu("Menu") { ... } }' to inject global commands on the Mac.

title: visionOS & Spatial Computing
theory: visionOS ushers in Spatial Computing (Apple Vision Pro). It introduces the Z-axis (depth), Windows (2D/3D windows), Volumes (3D objects bounded in a box) and Immersive Spaces (full VR). SwiftUI is the foundation for the 2D/3D UI, and RealityKit is used to render immersive 3D scenes and anchor entities in the real world.
corporateCase: An interior design app uses an 'Immersive Space' to project a 3D sofa in the center of the user's real room using RealityKit, measuring collisions with the real walls.
gameCase: A chess game on visionOS floats a 3D 'Volume' in the middle of the user's room. It uses Hand Tracking so the player can physically grab and move the pieces.

exercises.question: Which Apple framework primarily handles physics rendering and 3D objects on visionOS?

quiz.question: What is a 'Volume' in visionOS?
options: A bounded 3D container (bounding box) that coexists with other apps and objects in the user's room
A mode that turns off camera Pass-through
quiz.explanation: Unlike a full Immersive Space, the Volume lets you render 3D models that share the user's physical space with other apps (shared windows).
